question: On 10 October 2016, the Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) between the EU and five countries in eastern and southern Africa entered into force, under which the EU allows 100 % duty-free access to all imports from the countries concerned. This situation is detrimental to European producers, in particular Spanish ones, who adhere to higher standards than their South African counterparts.
This means their produce is more expensive. Many of the products concerned are apparently in breach of the rules on the use of plant protection products laid down in Directive 91/414/EEC.

This situation is compounded by the fact that, since the entry into force of an agreement concluded in May 2023, Ukrainian grain can be brought into Spain with none of the limits or tariffs set for third-country imports into the EU. It is also produced at a far lower cost than Spanish grain: the costs our arable farmers have to put up with are much higher, and they are being forced to sell at a loss. 1.
Does the Commission intend to offer additional aid or compensation to European producers?
What steps will the Commission take to ensure that the interim EPA between the EU and the countries of eastern and southern Africa stops being detrimental to Spanish farming?
What steps will the Commission take to ensure that third countries comply with Directive 91/414/EEC?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.3.2024) 1. The Commission carefully monitors agricultural markets and stands ready to consider all policy tools available in case of serious market disturbances. Spain traditionally imports significant volumes of cereals for its livestock sector (7-8 million tonnes per year) as its domestic production is not sufficient to meet its needs.

Besides, droughts affected the last two Spanish harvests. Imports from July 2023 to January 2024 reached 9.4 million tonnes, including 6.2 million tonnes from Ukraine. These imports fulfil the Spanish demand. Spanish cereal prices remain among the highest in the EU. 2.

Madagascar, Mauritius, Seychelles and Zimbabwe apply the Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) with Eastern and Southern Africa since 2012 and Comoros since 2019. Agricultural imports from those countries already enjoyed duty-free, quota-free treatment before the EPA.

Nevertheless, the EPA includes a safeguard clause in case imports from a party would cause or threaten to cause serious injury or serious disturbances to the domestic industry. In addition, the EU trade defence instruments can tackle dumped or subsidised imports harming EU producers. Any EU industry harmed by unfairly traded imports may seek advice from the Directorate-General for Trade. 3.

Regulation (EC) No 1107/20091 repealed Directive 91/414/EEC2 in 2011. The scope of this Regulation is limited to the marketing and use of plant protection products in the EU. Food and feed imported into the EU from third countries must comply with the maximum pesticide residue levels (MRLs) set out in Regulation (EC) No 396/20053 and all other EU import requirements.
Those requirements are not more favourable than those applicable to EU products.
1 Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 21 October 2009 concerning

the placing of plant protection products on the market and repealing Council Directives 79/117/EEC and 91/414/EEC. 2 Council Directive 91/414/EEC of 15 July 1991 concerning the placing of plant protection products on the market. 3 Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 February 2005 on maximum residue levels of pesticides in or on food and feed of plant and animal origin and amending Council Directive 91/414/EEC.
